newsitem.title: HONG KONG: US boycott deals blow to China's HK assembly plan.
newsitem.headline: US boycott deals blow to China's HK assembly plan.

text.p: The United States blew a hole in China's plans by boycotting the investiture of Hong Kong's new unelected legislature when Beijing takes over from Britain in three weeks time, diplomats said on Tuesday.

Hong Kong's future leader Tung Chee-hwa is to swear in the Provisional Legislature in the early hours of July 1 after a midnight handover ceremony that will end 156 years of British colonial rule and raise China's red flag over Hong Kong.
Britain and its Western allies have attacked the new assembly, questioning its legitimacy and a need for it to replace the democratically elected Legislative Council.

The 60-strong provisional assembly, which has met so far in China because of doubts about its legality, is packed with pro-China politicians and businessmen picked by a China-controlled committee six months ago.
In Washington, U.S. State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns said Secretary of State Madeline Albright, who will be a guest at the handover ceremony, would not go to the swearing-in.
"I can tell you if she were invited, she would not attend that ceremony...because it wouldn't be appropriate," Burns said.

A Western diplomat said: "If China hoped to have a big parade of leaders to bless the swearing-in of this questionable legislature, Albright's move will blow a hole in this. It is likely other Western countries will follow her lead."
British Governor Chris Patten hinted other Western leaders might behave the same way, but he left the world guessing about whether Prime Minister Tony Blair would attend the handover.
Speculation is rife that Blair might boycott the event if China tries to humiliate Britain by inaugurating the legislature under the eyes of VIP handover guests.

"We know that the United States feels strongly about the provisional legislature and I guess that some other political leaders who believe in democracy and democratic institutions will have the same sort of concerns," Patten told reporters.
He dodged a question about how Blair might act and recalled Britain's firm opposition to the provisional legislature. "I suggest you draw your own conclusions," he said.
"No decision has been taken yet," British Foreign Office spokesman in Hong Kong Bill Dickson told Reuters.
Diplomatic sources said the delay on a decision by Blair was linked to the swearing-in and that London appeared to be awaiting clarification from China on the ceremonies.

Future leader Tung, a tycoon chosen to run Hong Kong by a China-controlled electoral college, told Britain's Independent Television News in an interview on Monday that he was ready to resign if the job clashed with his principles.
Tung's comment came just a week after his future number-two, Chief Secretary Anson Chan, made a similar statement, arousing speculation about tension between the two leaders.
"I would resign on matters of principle. We would all do it because it is important, as a person we all have our principles. We all have our vision. We all have our beliefs," Tung said.
"I am 60 years old already and in the 60 years that is one thing I have learnt, to stand up for principles, to stand up for one's beliefs, to stand up for one's visions," Tung said.

Tung reiterated statements he has made lately calling for an end to anti-Beijing pro-democracy protests in Hong Kong. Last week 50,000 people gathered to honour the victims killed in China's 1989 anti-democracy crackdown by the army in Beijing.

A Hong Kong newspaper quoted Beijing sources as saying President Jiang Zemin would come to the handover with Premier Li Peng. Jiang would be the first Chinese leader ever to set foot in Hong Kong, which Britain wrested from the imperial Chinese Qing dynasty in the 19th century Opium Wars.
